summaries.example: Imagine seeing a large dog run toward you. You may notice what is happening, feel afraid, and want to move away. Medieval thinkers asked whether the fear begins in your body, your feelings, your thoughts, or all of these together. They also asked whether you are responsible for the first frightened reaction or only for what you choose to do next.
summaries.summary: Medieval philosophers built their theories of emotions from older Greek and Roman ideas, especially those of Plato and Aristotle. They wanted to understand what an emotion is and how it relates to thinking, the body, choice, and moral behavior. Some described emotions as movements of lower or sensory parts of the soul. Others emphasized the will, the power connected with choosing. Aristotle’s approach treated an emotion as a group of connected features: a way of seeing something as good or bad, a felt response, a tendency to act, and bodily changes. Medieval writers also made lists and systems for sorting emotions. Avicenna described special powers that recognize emotionally important things and start action. Aquinas developed a detailed classification, while Bonaventure and later John Duns Scotus gave more attention to emotions connected with the intellectual will. The discussions did not all agree. Some thinkers valued control over emotion, while others argued that emotions can be educated so they support a good life. Compassion became especially important in medieval theology: feeling concern for another person’s suffering could lead to helping. A major question was whether an unchosen first reaction is blameworthy or whether blame requires free consent.
key_ideas: Plato thought reason should guide emotional parts that seek pleasure or react strongly.
Aristotle said an emotion can include a judgment, a pleasant or unpleasant feeling, a push toward action, and body changes.
Many medieval thinkers studied how emotions begin, how the body is involved, and how people can guide them.
A quick feeling may not be a chosen action. Some thinkers said responsibility begins when a person freely agrees to or continues it.
Thomas Aquinas organized emotions into groups such as love, desire, joy, fear, courage, anger, and distress.
summaries.why_it_matters: These old discussions help us ask lasting questions about feelings and responsibility. They show that an emotion may involve thoughts, body changes, feelings, and urges at the same time. They also suggest that emotions are not simply enemies of reason: with practice, they may support kindness and good choices. Studying different medieval views teaches us how philosophical ideas develop through disagreement and careful comparison.

important_terms.definition: A feeling or reaction such as fear, joy, anger, love, or sadness. Medieval writers often called emotions “passions.”
The part of a person that can think, choose, feel, and act. Medieval philosophers used different models of the soul.
A picture or idea of what is happening, such as noticing that something is dangerous or helpful.
A first reaction that appears before a person has freely chosen it.
A helpful habit of feeling and acting in a good way. Aristotle connected virtues with training emotions and practical thinking.

questions_to_think_about: Is a first feeling something you choose?
When might a feeling help you make a good decision?
Can people train their emotional habits?
Should a person be judged for a feeling, an action, or both?

summaries.example: Suppose a student learns that a friend has been treated unfairly. The student may judge the situation as wrong, feel anger, experience bodily excitement, and be moved to confront the problem. Aquinas could analyze these as connected features of an emotion, while Scotus might also ask how the student’s will is affected by the situation and whether the resulting pleasure or distress is freely chosen. The first reaction and the later decision to act need not have the same moral status.
summaries.summary: The entry traces medieval theories of emotion from their ancient sources through late medieval debates. Plato distinguished rational, spirited, and appetitive dimensions of the soul and treated uncontrolled impulses as a source of weakness in action. Aristotle offered a compositional analysis: an occurrent emotion involves an evaluative cognition, a felt affect, an impulse toward behavior, and characteristic physiological responses. Stoic writers instead treated emotions primarily as erroneous judgments about value and recommended apatheia, freedom from emotion. Medieval authors knew this model but generally preserved a distinction between intellectual reason and lower or sensory emotional powers. They also combined Platonic, Aristotelian, Stoic, medical, and Christian materials in increasingly systematic taxonomies. Avicenna’s faculty psychology became especially influential: inner senses identify emotionally relevant intentions, while concupiscible and irascible powers produce motivational responses. Thirteenth-century thinkers sought a coherent basis for classifying contrary emotions, often invoking pleasant or painful objects and the notion of arduousness. Albert the Great and Aquinas treated emotions as acts of sensory moving powers. Aquinas’s taxonomy organized love, desire, joy, hate, aversion, distress, hope, despair, fear, courage, and anger according to their objects and modes of movement. Bonaventure, and more systematically Scotus, challenged the sharp boundary between sensory emotion and intellectual willing. Scotus described joy and distress as passions of the will: they are states of the intellectual power caused by an object and not directly produced by free choice. Later thinkers disagreed about whether liking, volition, pleasure, and love are free acts
key_ideas: Plato’s tripartite psychology placed reason, spirited motivation, and appetite in tension; Aristotle gave a more detailed account of emotions as structured psychological events.

Stoic theory reduced emotions to mistaken value judgments and aimed at freedom from emotion, whereas Platonist and Aristotelian approaches usually retained emotional powers and sought moderation or education.
Avicenna explained emotion through faculties, including inner senses that recognize emotionally significant features and motivational powers that can lead to action.
Thirteenth-century authors developed taxonomies using contrasts such as pleasant versus painful and ordinary versus difficult or arduous objects.
Aquinas treated emotions as acts of sensory motivational powers and classified them into eleven major types, while Bonaventure and Scotus extended emotional language to the intellectual will.
Medieval debates about first movements, consent, and compassion connected emotion theory to ethics: spontaneous reactions may differ from freely sustained or chosen responses.
summaries.why_it_matters: The medieval debate anticipates central issues in contemporary philosophy of emotion: whether emotions are cognitive, embodied, motivational, or some combination; whether they are passive events or partly voluntary; and how they relate to moral responsibility. Its taxonomies also show that classification is theoretical rather than merely descriptive: the categories chosen—faculty, object, bodily movement, felt quality, or difficulty—shape the resulting account. The discussions of compassion and moral education further raise the question of whether good character requires suppressing emotions, regulating them, or cultivating appropriate emotional responses.

important_terms.definition: A psychological reaction involving an evaluative representation, felt pleasantness or unpleasantness, an action tendency, and often physiological change; theories emphasize these elements differently.
A medieval term for a passion or affective state, often understood as something undergone rather than freely produced.
A power or capacity of the soul responsible for a kind of activity, such as sensory perception, motivation, imagination, or intellectual willing.
A representation of something as emotionally relevant, such as dangerous, beneficial, difficult, or harmful; in some theories it initiates motivation.
The motivational power directed toward sensory good and evil. In medieval taxonomies it is contrasted with the irascible power.
The motivational power concerned with difficult or threatening goods and evils, often involving struggle, resistance, or approach.
The intellectual power of choosing or refusing. Late medieval thinkers debated whether it can itself have passions or quasi-emotional states.
Free agreement to a thought, desire, or proposed action. In Augustinian discussions, consent helps distinguish an involuntary temptation from a culpable act.

questions_to_think_about: Does an emotion require a judgment, or can bodily change and impulse be sufficient?
Is moderation a better goal than eliminating emotion?
What does the distinction between a first movement and consent contribute to moral responsibility?
Are pleasure and love necessarily different states when a goal is achieved?
Would a theory centered on sensory faculties explain emotions in the will adequately?

summaries.example: Picture a student who sees a classmate being left out. The student notices the unfairness, feels upset, and wants to help. Medieval philosophers might separate these parts: the judgment about the situation, the feeling, the urge to act, and bodily changes such as a faster heartbeat. They might also ask whether the first feeling was chosen, and whether the student later decided to help. Different theories would explain the same event in different ways.
summaries.summary: Medieval theories of emotion grew out of ancient Greek and Roman philosophy, especially Plato and Aristotle. Plato described the soul as having rational, spirited, and appetitive aspects. His model emphasized the need for reason to guide strong impulses. Aristotle offered a more detailed explanation of an emotion as a combination of an evaluation, a pleasant or unpleasant feeling, a tendency toward action, and bodily changes. The Stoics developed a different approach: they treated emotions mainly as mistaken judgments about what is valuable and aimed at freedom from emotion. Medieval thinkers knew these views but usually continued to distinguish emotional powers from the intellect. Over time, they added ideas from medicine, Christian theology, and Avicenna’s faculty psychology. Avicenna explained that inner senses recognize emotionally important features and that motivational faculties respond to them. This helped medieval writers study both animal and human behavior, including the difference between instinctive reactions and responses involving human concepts. Scholars also tried to build taxonomies. Some organized emotions by present or future good and evil; others used liking and dislike, or distinguished ordinary objects from arduous ones that are difficult to obtain or avoid. Aquinas developed the most extensive medieval system, dividing emotions into concupiscible and irascible groups and arranging them by their objects and movements. Bonaventure and John Duns Scotus challenged the idea that emotions belong only to sensory powers. Scotus argued that the will can undergo joy and distress caused by objects, even though these states are not directly free choices. Across these debates, thinkers examined moral education, compassion, temptation, and responsibility. They
key_ideas: Ancient theories strongly shaped medieval thinking, but medieval authors added new psychological, medical, ethical, and theological questions.
Aristotle described emotions through several connected parts: an evaluation, a feeling, an urge to act, and bodily effects.
Avicenna’s theory used faculties and inner senses to explain how people and animals recognize what matters emotionally.
Medieval scholars disagreed about how to divide emotions, especially between concupiscible reactions to ordinary goods or evils and irascible reactions involving difficult challenges.
Aquinas created a detailed classification, while Bonaventure and Scotus gave more attention to emotions of the intellectual will.
Many thinkers distinguished an involuntary first reaction from freely consenting to or continuing that reaction.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history matters because it shows that questions about emotions are not new. Philosophers have long asked whether feelings contain beliefs, whether bodies or thoughts come first, and how much control people have over their reactions. The medieval distinction between an immediate response and later consent is especially useful for thinking about responsibility. The tradition also presents two possible goals: eliminating disruptive emotions or educating them so they support reason, virtue, and concern for other people.

important_terms.definition: A feeling and response such as fear, anger, joy, love, or distress. Medieval authors often used the word “passion” for an emotion.
A capacity or part of the soul that performs a particular job, such as sensing, imagining, remembering, moving, or choosing.
A thought or perception that presents something as good, bad, dangerous, helpful, or otherwise important to the person.
A quick emotional response that happens before deliberate choice or agreement.
The power to choose or refuse. Some late medieval thinkers argued that the will can have emotional states too.
A system for organizing items into groups. Medieval philosophers created several different taxonomies of emotions.
A difficult good or evil that takes effort to gain, avoid, overcome, or resist. It became important in some medieval emotion classifications.

questions_to_think_about: Can an emotion be both a feeling and a kind of judgment?
Why might philosophers want to make a complete list of emotions?
Should fear of a real danger count as a mistake, as some Stoics suggested?
How might practice change a person’s emotional habits?
Can the will have feelings, or only choices?
